items.reason: The asynchronous legacy writes inherit request cancellation and can be aborted after the response completes.
Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the committed-result wrapper, allowing updates to be recomputed against stale legacy state.
Successful Delete uses the object name as the metric's kind label, creating per-object series.
The tests share backend mocks and never wait for or verify asynchronous legacy writes, so removing those writes would still pass.
The Create test name incorrectly says only unified storage is written despite the legacy write.
The List error test still says listing is unimplemented although it tests propagation of a storage error.
Background legacy writes use the request context and can be canceled when the HTTP handler finishes.
Independent legacy-write goroutines can execute out of commit order, leaving stale or resurrected objects.
Storage.Create and Storage.Update failure branches record legacy durations, misattributing storage errors and latency.
Delete's success metric passes name instead of options.Kind, splitting labels and creating per-object series.
Legacy.DeleteCollection uses recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, attributing legacy latency and failures to storage.
Delete installs d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger in the context, losing operation fields downstream.
The asynchronous legacy mirror inherits request cancellation, so successful primary writes can leave legacy writes canceled.
Passing original objInfo to Legacy.Update recomputes the update against legacy state instead of forwarding the committed primary result through updateWrapper.
